gradients.purpose: Iridescent film: the five foundation fills as one gradient. Defined in the stylesheet as a token and a utility; no shipped surface uses it (the recorder tape draws its level in ink).

gradients.name: highlighter
gradients.value: linear-gradient(transparent 14%, <fill> 14%, <fill> 92%, transparent 92%) on the lyric sheet; on the review page linear-gradient(transparent 10%, <band> 10%, <band> 92%, transparent 92%), where <band> is color-mix(in oklch, <fill> 65%, transparent) for a strength at rest and the foundation fill when its note is in focus; mix-blend-mode: multiply
gradients.purpose: The band behind noted words. On the review page a band means a strength, in its own foundation's fill in every view (the first strength's fill where a word carries several, unless another is in focus). Something to work on is never a band: it is a 2px ink underline, 3px in its foundation's ink while its note is in focus.

shadows.name: glass-lit

shadows.name: overlay

motion.name: ease-out

motion.name: ridge-dim
motion.purpose: Non-current ridges dim while a take plays.

motion.name: word-fill
motion.purpose: Spoken words fill to ink as the playhead passes: from 35% ink on the lyric sheet, from ink-3 on the review page.

motion.name: ghost-drift
motion.purpose: Dashed ridge outlines of an unpressed sleeve drift. Off under reduced motion.

motion.name: nav-scroll
motion.purpose: Nav turns translucent with a bottom edge after 8px of scroll.

motion.name: follow-playhead
motion.value: per frame, scroll by 12% of the distance between the playhead and 42% of the viewport height
motion.purpose: The review page follows the playhead; wheel, touch or scroll keys release it, Follow restores it. Under reduced motion it jumps line by line.

motion.name: tape-scan
motion.purpose: A glass head sweeps the recorded tape left to right and back while the coach listens. Rests at the start under reduced motion.

motion.name: slice-focus
motion.purpose: Scrubber note slices come to full strength for the note in focus (80% on hover). On the review page a noted phrase switches at once between its resting mark and its focus mark (the full band, or the 3px underline in the foundation ink).

motion.name: margin-bar-focus
motion.purpose: The margin bar of a several-line note goes to the full foundation ink when its note is in focus or hovered. At rest a strength's bar is its foundation ink at 55%; a bar for something to work on is line-strong, or its foundation ink at 40% with one foundation in view.

narrative.overview:
**Creative North Star: "The Liner Booklet"**

Each lesson unfolds like the liner booklet of an album from a Night City label. The take is the track, its transcript is the lyric sheet, and the review is written under its lines. Every section is a booklet spread: graphite album covers and titles on the left, white pages of reading on the right. The cover is not an illustration; it is drawn from the take itself: one ridge for each spoken line that showed a strength, raised by that line's recorded level and filled with the foundation of that strength. Ridges stack up from the bottom, so a take with few strengths is a low stack and covers fill up as you practise. The one exception is the promotional sleeve, which shows every foundation at once.

The notebook is an undertone, not the personality, and it lives in structure only: notes written under the line they are about, one endless page per take, and the 8px rhythm. It has no material of its own; booklet pages are plain white, and dotted surfaces read cheap rather than chic. Everything else is the label's: wide extra-bold Archivo that names things, Martian Mono for timecodes, measurements, catalog numbers and track numbers, neutral graphite sleeves, and orange glass as the one warm light. Color is rationed. Foundation hues appear only where a foundation is in the data, laid on words as multiplied highlighter and on ridges as fill. Small orange details tie the pages together: glass marks every play control and whatever is happening now.

The voice sells the outcome, not the instrument: unlocking your voice, confidence, potential, learning and getting better. Covers are brand texture and are never named as a feature in copy. The first view stays sparse, so nothing competes with listening to the example.

The page has one rhythm. A single twelve-column spread runs top to bottom; sections separate by space and by ground (paper, white surface, graphite), never by rules. One shared playhead drives everything that follows a take: the lyric sheet fills in word by word, the cover's other ridges dim while a glass bead rides the current crest, and a glass hairline tracks progress.

Where the landing reads a take as a lyric sheet, the review reads it line by line under its timeline. The review is one long white booklet page under a sticky graphite transport whose scrubber is the take's only timeline: the glass playhead runs along the top and the notes sit on the bar as foundation slices. On the page, each spoken line sits beside its timecode, silences open real space, and every note is written once, under the line it begins on; a note that runs over several lines draws a bar down the margin beside them. Strengths and things to work on are told apart by one grammar: filled for a strength, open for something to work on. Colour on the words is earned: a strength is a band in its foundation's fill, and something to work on is an ink underline. One note is in focus at a time: it alone is open, quoting its words on its own foundation fill. Reading a note and hearing it are separate: opening one never starts the audio. The recorder is a horizontal tape: one minute, left to right, filling with your level as you speak. Covers do not appear on the upload and review screens.

The landing's lyric sheet is the earlier of the two readings and keeps its own marks: every noted word wears its foundation's band, strength or not; words not yet spoken wait at 35% ink; notes sit two across under the line and play when pressed; and silences print their seconds. The rules below say which surface they cover.
keyCharacteristics: Booklet spreads on a 12-column grid: covers and titles in the left five columns (sticky on large screens), reading in the right seven.

Album covers drawn from the take: graphite ground, one filled ridge per line that showed a strength, stacked from the bottom and clipped at a horizon, title on clean graphite below; covers fill up as you practise.
Plain white booklet pages with a 10px corner; the notebook lives in structure (notes under their line, one endless page per take, the 8px rhythm), never in a printed texture.

Foundation fills as multiplied highlighter on words: on the landing lyric sheet behind every noted word, on the review only where the colour is earned (a band in its foundation's fill for a strength, an ink underline for something to work on); pins filled or open, solid or dashed.

One grammar for the two kinds of note on the review: a strength is filled (a band on the words, a filled pin with a tick, a filled lane slice, a filled swatch), something to work on is open (a 2px ink underline, an open pin with an upward arrow, an open lane slice, an open swatch).
Orange glass for play controls and whatever is live: the play buttons, the current word, the bead, the playheads, recording, the section you are in.
Wide Archivo names things; Martian Mono numbers them.
One timeline per take: the transport scrubber with foundation note slices and a glass playhead, which the review page follows.
The recorder tape: one minute left to right, the recorded level as a mirrored ink area.
Foundations the review did not assess are drawn dashed, never filled.

rules.name: The Active-Only Rule
rules.body: A foundation color appears only where that foundation is present in the data: a ridge whose line showed it as its first strength, a highlighted word, a lane, a pin, a swatch. Never as section tint or brand accent. The single exception is a promotional cover (the hero sleeve): the take is cut into five even slices, one per foundation fill in course order, every ridge filled. No other surface borrows the five fills as decoration. A 10px swatch also stands beside a foundation's name wherever the foundation is named as a subject or a choice (the recorder's "The coach listens for" list, the notes-switch chips, the lesson page header); that is a label, not decoration.

rules.name: The One Warm Light Rule
rules.body: Orange glass marks two things only: play controls, and whatever is live. Play controls are glass at rest as well as while playing, as small orange details that tie the pages together. Live means the playhead and everything it drives (the current word, the cover's bead, the progress hairline), recording, and the section in view. Until a take has been started, the cover shows no bead and the sheet shows no underline; once started they stay on the current line and word, playing or paused. The same light answers the reader's own input: keyboard focus rings, the caret, the text selection and the ring around a drop target. No orange on anything else.

rules.name: The Not Judged Rule
rules.body: All five foundations are reviewed, but a foundation the review returns as uncertain (not enough evidence on this take) is drawn with a dashed line-strong swatch, its name in ink-3, and the backend's own reason ("There is not enough clear speech to judge volume in this take."), falling back to "Not enough evidence to judge on this take"; it gets no verdict, no lane and no fill. Only judged foundations carry their pair. Not judged must never read as passed.

rules.name: The No Brown Rule
rules.body: Dark surfaces are neutral graphite (chroma 0.004 or less); inks and shadow tints stay at chroma 0.01 or less. No brown or walnut surfaces, text or shadows; shadows tint neutral. Orange glass is the only warm color. This is a founder decision recorded in PRODUCT.md.

rules.name: The Fill and Ink Rule
rules.body: Every foundation hue is a pair: pastel for fields, deep ink for text, strokes and pins. Pastel never carries text by itself; foundation text is always the ink.

rules.name: The Colour Is Earned Rule
rules.body: On the review, colour on the words of a line means a strength (founder decision, 2026-10-03: the mixed "All notes" view must itself tell good from bad; a grey band against a grey underline, and a small "Effective" label, were not enough). A strength is a band in its own foundation's fill, in every view: at 65% at rest, and at the full fill when its note is in focus (being played, picked or stepped to; hovering a note or its margin bar previews it), the way a cover fills with colour as strengths are earned. Something to work on is never a band: it is a 2px ink underline, which becomes a 3px underline in its foundation's ink only while its note is in focus. A word shows one fill at most (founder decision, 2026-10-03: one stripe per overlapping note, with "continues from" markers, could not be read): when a word carries more than one strength, the first one's fill shows unless another is in focus. Overlap is resolved by the notes switch and by focus, never by layering colours. The note in focus has its words to itself (founder decision, 2026-10-03): while a note is open or previewed, other notes' bands and underlines on those words step back, and return when it closes. Suggested-phrase underlines, the dashed "a pause belongs here" box and the pauses-ink pause bar show only for the note in focus or, with one foundation in view, for that foundation's notes. This rule covers the review only. The landing lyric sheet is built differently and is recorded as it is: there every noted word, strength or something to work on, wears the band of the first note on it, and a second note on the same word adds a 2px underline in its ink.

rules.name: The Filled or Open Rule
rules.body: Strengths and things to work on are told apart by one grammar on the review (founder decision, 2026-10-03): filled means a strength, open means something to work on. Pins: a disc filled with the foundation ink carrying a white tick, or an open ring (surface inside a 1.5px ring of the ink) carrying an upward arrow in the ink. Words: a band in the foundation's fill, like a highlighter (keep this), or an ink underline, like an editor's mark. Foundation rows: a swatch filled with the fill when the foundation's verdict is effective, or an open swatch (surface inside a 1.5px ink ring) when there is something to work on. Foundation lanes: a slice filled with the fill, or an open slice (surface inside the ink ring). Transport slices: filled with the fill, or an open outline in the fill. On a note entry the pin alone shows the kind (founder decision, 2026-10-03: the two fixed sides and the legend above the first line were removed, because a line with only strengths left their place on the right with nothing to stand against, and the words "strength" and "to work on" were more to read). The tick and the arrow back up filled and open, so the kind never rests on fill alone, and the entry's accessible label still says it in words. The notes switch shows the band and underline marks on its "Strengths" and "To work on" chips. The landing lyric sheet shares only the pin: filled for a strength, an open ring for something to work on, with no tick or arrow.

rules.name: The Mono Numbers Rule
rules.body: Martian Mono sets numbers that belong to the take or the label: timecodes, measured values, catalog numbers, track numbers. Words are never set in mono; a unit that belongs to a number ("s", "×") travels with it, but counted nouns do not ("4 notes" sets only the 4 in mono). Token names in the showcase's colour swatches are code and are set in mono. Drift, not precedent: the build still sets a word in mono in three places (the cover's take line "Take 1 · 0:15", the recorder's "of 01:00", and the showcase scrubber's "Arrow keys move 0.1 s").

rules.name: The Sentence-Case Rule
rules.body: Labels are small, semibold and sentence case. The build has no uppercase tracked labels and no eyebrows above headings.

rules.name: The 4px Leading Rule
rules.body: Line heights for text that sits beside other rows land on whole 4px steps (16, 20, 24, 28, 40px), so text rows sit on the page's cadence.

rules.name: The Under the Line Rule
rules.body: A review note sits under the line it is about, never in a side column beside it (founder decision, 2026-10-03: notes on the right were hard to connect with the words; below the text, as on the landing lyric sheet, is preferred). Under each line are one-line entries, one for every note that begins on that line, as one list in every view (founder decision, 2026-10-03: the two fixed sides of the All notes view were removed; when a line had only strengths, their place on the right had nothing to stand against). A note that runs over several lines is written once, under the line it begins on, and is never listed again under later lines (founder decision, 2026-10-03); a bar in the margin runs beside every line it covers and through the silences between them, and that bar alone shows how far the note runs: the entry carries no line count. Only the note in focus is open: it adds the words it is about, quoted in its own foundation fill so note and text can be matched by eye, then the why, the practice line and the suggestions. It does not print the observation (founder decision, 2026-10-03: the sentence repeated what the rule label and the quote already say); the observation stays in the entry's accessible label. A several-line note picked on a later line, by its words or its bar, shows its open card under that line too for as long as it is open there. A line's row holds its words and its notes; silence stays its own row, so the room notes take is never read as time.

rules.name: The Read or Hear Rule
rules.body: On the review, reading a note and hearing it are separate (founder decision, 2026-10-03: reading a note must not start the audio). Pressing a noted phrase, a margin bar or a note's line opens the note and never plays; pressing the open note again closes it. Hearing has its own controls: the glass play triangle with the mono time on the right of each note, the suggestion buttons inside an open note, a line's timecode, and the transport, whose note slices open their note and play it. Playing a note from its own control also opens it. The landing lyric sheet does not separate the two: there a note is one button that plays its passage.

rules.name: The Lines Are Edges or Data Rule
rules.body: A one-pixel line is either the edge of an object (a page's ring, a lane well, the scrolled nav's bottom border) or a piece of data (the progress track, the retake spine, the pause leader, a dashed empty slot, the scrubber track, the silence leader's dash, the recorder tape's bare remainder). Rows, notes, list items and page sections never get a divider; they separate by space on the grid. One hairline is neither edge nor data: the 20px line between the two groups of the review's notes switch (founder decision, 2026-10-03), which parts two kinds of filter inside one control and is not a pattern for dividing content. The 3px margin bar of a several-line note is data: it is the note's extent.

rules.name: The Two Drops Rule
rules.body: Large soft shadows belong to covers (sleeve) and booklet pages. Nothing else on the page lifts. The sticky transport is flat graphite with no shadow or rule. Overlays are not on the page: a dialog or a sheet floats over it on the overlay shadow.

dos: **Do** build every section as a spread on the 12-column grid: cover or title in the left five columns, reading in the right seven.

**Do** draw a take's cover from the take: one ridge per line that showed a strength, from its level, filled with that foundation, stacked from the bottom on full-cover slots, clipped at the horizon, title on clean graphite below. Only a promotional sleeve fills every ridge.
**Do** put reading on plain white booklet pages with the 10px corner.

**Do** mark noted words with the foundation fill as multiplied highlighter, and set foundation text in its ink; in the review's lines only a strength earns the band, while on the landing lyric sheet every noted word wears it.

**Do** let colour on the review's words mean a strength: a band in its own foundation's fill in every view (65% at rest, the full fill in focus). Mark something to work on with a 2px ink underline, which takes its foundation's ink at 3px only while its note is in focus. Resolve overlap with the notes switch and one note in focus.

**Do** keep a line's review notes in one list under it in every view, and let the pin say the kind: a filled disc with a tick for a strength, an open ring with an upward arrow for something to work on.

**Do** tell strengths from things to work on the same way across the review: filled for a strength (band, filled pin, filled lane slice, filled swatch), open for something to work on (underline, open pin, open lane slice, open swatch); on a note the pin's tick or arrow says the kind, and the accessible label says it in words.
**Do** keep reading and hearing apart on the review: words, margin bars and note lines open a note; only play controls start the audio.
**Do** drive the sheet, the cover and the progress hairline from one playhead, with glass only on play controls and what is current.
**Do** set timecodes, measurements, catalog numbers and track numbers in Martian Mono with tabular figures.
**Do** keep layout spacing on 8px steps and text line heights on whole 4px steps.
**Do** keep honesty about the example in the footer and on illustrated data (the dashed "Illustration" badge), and leave a dashed empty slot where a take does not exist yet.
**Do** sell the outcome in copy: unlocking your voice, confidence, potential, learning and getting better.
**Do** keep the first view sparse: headline, one outcome line, "Try a free review" and "See an example", the cover, then the example.
**Do** turn off ridge-rise, ghost-drift and the tape scan under reduced motion, and let a following page jump line by line instead of easing.

**Do** lay the review out as one long page under the transport: timecode and line per row, silences as space, each note written once under the line it begins on, one line each, a margin bar beside the lines a longer note covers, only the note in focus open and quoting its words in its own foundation fill, the scrubber as the only timeline.
**Do** draw foundations that could not be judged with a dashed swatch and their own reason, never filled.
**Do** release the page from the playhead the moment the reader scrolls, and offer Follow to bring it back.
donts: **Don't** use a foundation hue for decoration, section backgrounds, or emphasis unrelated to that foundation; the promotional sleeve is the only exception.
**Don't** present covers as a feature in copy; they are brand texture.
**Don't** put credits, verdict tables, badges or explanatory captions near the hero cover, or anything else that competes with listening to the example.
**Don't** use glass on anything that is neither a play control nor live.
**Don't** draw lines between list rows, notes, takes or page sections; lines are object edges or data.
**Don't** put review notes in a side margin (the margin holds only the bars of several-line notes), sort them into fixed sides by kind, or label the room notes take as time; silence is its own row.
**Don't** layer several foundation colours on the same words of the review: no stripes, no stacked marks in different inks.
**Don't** put a band behind words to work on in the review's lines, or grey out a strength there: a band means a strength and wears its foundation's fill.

**Don't** explain overlap or kind with colour keys, legends or "continues" markers, and don't list a note again under later lines or mark it "from an earlier line"; it is written once, and its margin bar shows how far it runs.
**Don't** mark tentative on the review's words; it lives on the note's pin and label.

**Don't** make a review note say again what is already shown: no kind in words (the pin's tick or arrow says it), no line count (the margin bar shows it), no observation sentence in the open note (the rule label and the quote say it). These stay in the accessible label; notes on the lyric sheet keep their observation.
**Don't** add a ribbon, tape gutter or second timeline beside the review's lines; the transport scrubber is the only one. A margin bar marks which lines a note covers; it is not a timeline.
**Don't** start playback from a review note's line, its words or its margin bar; opening a note is silent. (On the landing lyric sheet a note is a play button.)
**Don't** put large shadows on anything on the page other than covers and booklet pages; only overlays (dialog, sheet) float on their own.
**Don't** set words in mono, or labels in uppercase with tracking; no eyebrows above headings.

**Don't** let the notebook become literal: no dot grids or dotted surfaces, ruled lines, binder rings, washi or sticky tape, handwriting fonts or stationery props. The notebook lives in structure only: notes under their line, one endless page per take, the 8px rhythm. (The recorder tape is the recorded take, an audio tape, and is native to the world.)
**Don't** round badges, tags or swatches into pills; keep them at 3px or less.
**Don't** use brown or walnut tones for surfaces, text or shadows; dark means neutral graphite.
